title: Short-Range Vector Spin Glasses: Parisi Hierarchies and Real-Space Ultrametricity
authors: Akash Vijay, Jaewon Kim, Jong Yeon Lee
abstract: Replica symmetry breaking (RSB) is the organizing principle of mean-field spin-glass theory, yet whether a continuous Parisi hierarchy can arise in a genuinely short-range system in finite spatial dimension remains unresolved. Here we introduce a disordered model of $N$-component vector spins on a $D$-dimensional hypercubic lattice, with random matrix couplings on nearest-neighbor links and random tensor couplings on elementary plaquettes. In the large-$N$ limit, the model supports thermodynamically stable one-step, full, and one-full RSB phases, alongside replica-symmetric paramagnetic and ferromagnetic phases. We find that spatial locality constrains these ordered phases through two distinct infrared mechanisms. ($i$) Quenched random anisotropy destroys uniform ferromagnetism for $D\leq4$ through an Imry-Ma mechanism. ($ii$) A continuous Parisi hierarchy gives rise to replica Goldstone modes whose gaplessness is protected by a Ward identity. At leading order in $1/N$, these modes behave as a band of free spin waves, producing infrared-divergent fluctuations in $D\leq2$ and a Mermin-Wagner instability of the continuously broken phase.   Remarkably, the Parisi hierarchy also acquires a direct real-space interpretation. For two pure states with mutual overlap $q$, a characteristic length $ξ(q)$ describes how far the differences between their frozen magnetization patterns remain correlated. Throughout a continuous sector of the Parisi hierarchy, $ξ(q)$ is independent of temperature and decreases monotonically with $q$. The ultrametric organization of pure states is therefore accompanied by an ultrametric hierarchy of real-space correlation lengths: states that separate near the root of the Parisi tree differ through long-wavelength frozen patterns, whereas states that separate farther from the root differ only on progressively shorter scales.
summary: This theoretical work investigates spin glasses with short-range interactions to determine if the mean-field Parisi theory applies. By analyzing a lattice spin model in the large-N limit, the authors prove that the continuous Parisi hierarchy is stable and, crucially, show that the abstract replica structure maps directly onto a real-space ultrametric organization of the system's pure states.
main_problem: The paper addresses whether the mean-field Parisi picture of replica symmetry breaking (RSB) can describe the low-temperature phase of spin glasses with strictly short-range interactions in finite dimensions.
main_result: The model supports thermodynamically stable RSB phases, and the Parisi hierarchy acquires a direct real-space interpretation showing an ultrametric organization of pure states via correlation lengths.
method: The analysis employs the replica method in the large-N limit, analyzing the saddle-point structure of the free energy and relating the abstract Parisi profile to physical correlation lengths.
model_or_system: The system is a disordered model of N-component vector spins on a D-dimensional hypercubic lattice, featuring random couplings on nearest-neighbor links and plaquettes.
key_observables: Edwards–Anderson order parameter ($q_{EA}$), Parisi profile $q(x)$, and the characteristic real-space correlation length $\xi(q)$ between pure states.
important_parameters: Dimension $D$, large-$N$ limit, temperature $T$, and the overlap $q$ between pure states.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the large-N limit and assumes the existence of stable RSB phases characterized by specific Parisi profiles (1RSB, FRSB, etc.).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the model Hamiltonian (link and plaquette couplings), phase structure diagrams showing instability regions in different dimensions, and diagrams linking the Parisi tree levels to the decay of real-space correlation functions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the short-range model, then analyzing the stability of various RSB phases using replica calculations, and finally establishing the direct correspondence between the abstract Parisi hierarchy and the real-space ultrametric organization of pure states.
why_interesting: The connection between the abstract mathematical structure of RSB (Parisi hierarchy) and concrete, measurable real-space correlations (correlation length $\xi(q)$) provides a powerful, physically intuitive framework for understanding glassy dynamics in finite dimensions.

FIG. 2. Representative Parisi profiles for the RS, 1RSB, FRSB, and 1FRSB phases. (a) In the RS phase, the Parisi profile is constant, q(x) = qEA. (b) In the 1RSB phase, q(x) jumps from 0 to the Edwards–Anderson overlap qEA at the breaking point m. (c) In the FRSB phase, q(x) varies continuously up to xc, where it reaches qEA and re- mains on the Edwards–Anderson plateau for x > xc. (d) In the 1FRSB phase, the continuous branch reaches qm at xc, followed by a plateau up to m and a finite jump to qEA. When xc = m, the intermediate plateau has zero width.
